headlines.title: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access to U.S. stocks
headlines.summary: Major Indian brokerages are providing retail investors access to U.S. stocks at a time when the local market has been battered.
headlines.article_text: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Major online investment platforms are unlocking access to U.S. stocks for millions of Indian retail investors. Groww, an Indian broking platform that accounts for over 29% of India's 46 million active clients on broking channels, rolled out the U.S. stock trading feature earlier this month. NVIDIA, SpaceX, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Micron and Meta are the most popular stocks among retail investors. INDIA - 2026/07/22: In this photo illustration, a Spacex logo is seen displayed on a smartphone with a NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) logo in the background. Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty Images Major Indian online investment platforms are unlocking access to U.S. stocks for millions of retail investors eager to diversify into global assets as the country's markets continue to underperform. Earlier, access to U.S. markets and exchange-traded funds was limited to wealthier Indians, via global banks and wealth management firms. Groww, an Indian investment platform that accounts for more than 29% of the country's 46 million active investors across stock brokerages, rolled out the U.S. equity trading feature earlier this month, Harsh Jain, chief operating officer and co-founder of the company, told CNBC. NVIDIA, SpaceX , Apple , Alphabet, Amazon , Micron and Meta are the most popular companies among early users, Jain said, whose firm has provided access to more than 10,000 U.S. stocks, exchange-traded funds and fractional share ownership. Zerodha, the second-largest trading platform with a 15% share of active clients as per NSE data, has also started beta testing access to U.S. stocks and plans to launch in a few weeks, the company told CNBC. Another popular brokerage with 6.7 million active retail clients, Angel One, is also reportedly planning to launch U.S. stock trading on its platform. There is a "big interest" among Indians to invest in U.S. stocks, especially in tech companies, Nitin Jain, chief executive and director at Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Singapore, told CNBC. He added that "retail investors like whatever goes up," pointing to the frenzy among Indian investors for investing in crypto a few years back. U.S. stocks in demand "There has always been latent demand in India for investing in global companies," Somnath Mukherjee, vice president of corporate development at Zerodha, told CNBC. He said that the underperformance of the Indian stock market over the past few years and the lack of local artificial intelligence champions is driving the demand for U.S offerings. The depreciation of the Indian rupee against the dollar is also pushing investors "to keep a part of their portfolio in another currency," Mukherjee said. India's benchmark stock index, the Nifty 50, has dropped nearly 13% since the start of the year while the S&P 500 has gained over 12%. Foreign investors are fleeing the country's markets, with a record $32.5 billion in outflows in direct equities since January, as per data from Indian depository NSDL, pressuring the stock market. With the absence of any major AI company and relatively expensive valuations, investors have picked markets such as South Korea and Taiwan over India, experts said. In August, resident Indians sent over $321 million overseas for investing in equity and debt , up 111% from a year ago, according to the Indian central bank's data. In the financial year ended March 2026, outward remittances for investments in equity and debt stood at $2.6 billion. While the retail outflows are a small fraction of India's currency reserves, the worry is that they rise exactly when the rupee is weak, and US markets look strong, and thereby "amplify pressure at the worst moment," Tanvi Kanchan, associate director, head of international business and strategy, Anand Rathi Shares & Stock Brokers said. Investment now accounts for about 11.7% of total outward remittances, up from 5.8% a year ago, so Indians are shifting from spending abroad to investing abroad, Kanchan said. The exit of foreign investors and rising energy bills due to the Iran war have already hit the Indian currency , warranting the central bank to step in. Kotak's Jain cautioned that as participation increases, the Indian regulator could have "second thoughts" around allowing retail access to U.S. markets. headlines.summary: Prosecutors aimed to charge Cassidy Hutchinson over testimony about President Trump's conduct the day of the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol riot by his supporters.
headlines.article_text: Cassidy Hutchinson: Grand jury doesn't indict Trump former aide Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., denied the Department of Justice's request to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson. Hutchinson was being targeted for alleged false statements in her testimony to a congressional committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol by Trump supporters. Hutchinson told lawmakers a second-hand account about President Donald Trump angrily lunging at a security aide after being told he could not go to the Capitol that day. Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump, testifies during a public hearing of the U.S. House Select Committee to investigate the January 6 Attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Capitol Hill in Washington, June 28, 2022. Evelyn Hockstein | Reuters A federal grand jury Tuesday rejected a request by the Department of Justice to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her 2022 congressional testimony about President Donald Trump 's conduct during the Jan. 6, 2021, mob attack on the U.S. Capitol, The Washington Post reported. Prosecutors in the DOJ's Civil Rights Division sought to charge Hutchinson with a crime based on claims she made false statements, MS NOW said, citing two people with knowledge of the case. Hutchinson told lawmakers a second-hand account about Trump angrily lunging at a security aide after being told he could not go to the Capitol that day. Senior DOJ lawyer Neville Hedley, without naming Hutchinson in open court, on Tuesday told Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., had rejected a requested indictment, The Post reported. It is extremely rare for a grand jury to refuse to indict when prosecutors present evidence of alleged crimes. But since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, federal prosecutors in Washington have several times failed to obtain a grand jury indictment they sought. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Trump must sit for deposition in BBC lawsuit by Dec. 11, judge orders Virginia state Sen. Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle In recent weeks, prosecutors have filed separate criminal cases in U.S. District Court in D.C. against former FBI Director James Comey and two former FBI officials with charging documents other than grand jury indictments. In both cases, the alleged conduct occurred years earlier. Typically in such cases, prosecutors would seek a grand jury indictment. Hutchinson testified in June 2022 to the House Select Committee that investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot by a mob of Trump supporters, whose attack delayed for hours the confirmation of Joe Biden's electoral victory in the 2020 election. She said that after Trump spoke at a rally outside the White House that preceded the attack, then-White House official Tony Ornato asked her, "Did you effing hear what happened in [the president's vehicle,] The Beast?" She testified that Ornato told her that when Trump got in the car, he was under the impression from his then-Chief of Staff Mark Meadows that they going to the Capitol, as he had claimed in his speech to supporters at the rally. When Robert Engel, the head of Trump's security detail, said the president could not go there because the area was not secure, Trump "had a very strong, a very angry response to that," Hutchinson testified that Ornato said. "Tony described him as being irate," Hutchinson said, noting that Trump had said something like: "I'm the effing president, take me up to the Capitol now," according to Ornato. When Engel refused again to drive him to the Capitol, Trump "reached up towards the front of the vehicle to grab at the steering wheel. Mr. Engel grabbed his arm, said, 'Sir, you need to take your hand off the steering wheel. We're going back to the West Wing,'" Hutchinson testified. Trump "then used his free hand to lunge toward Bobby Engel," Hutchinson said she was told by Ornato. Correction: Neville Hedley is a senior DOJ lawyer. An earlier version misspelled his name.
